title: Localization of the polynomial-module good locus
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq0$, and $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. For a $P$-module $N$, let $G_R(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] be the union of $D(f)=\{\mathfrak p:f\notin\mathfrak p\}$ over $f\in R$ such that $N_f$ is free over $R_f$ [def-weil-pbc-free-module] and finitely presented over $R_f[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ [def-sc-finitely-presented-module]. Here $R_f=R[1/f]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], $N_f$ is the localization of the underlying $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away], and the polynomial action is $x_i(m/f^a)=(x_im)/f^a$. For every $P$-module $M$ and every $h\in R$, under the identification $\operatorname{Spec}(R_h)\cong D(h)$ induced by taking inverse images of prime ideals, one has $$G_{R_h}(M_h)=D(h)\cap G_R(M).$$ On the left the same definition is made using $R_h$ as base and $M_h$ as an $R_h[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$-module. No reducedness, finiteness, or nonzero-ring assumption is imposed.

source.place: Tag 051X (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-localize), specialized to the polynomial algebra; equations equation-flat-and-finitely-presented and equation-good-locus. The polynomial algebra is automatically free and finitely presented over the base.

proof.text: First record the coefficient-localization identification used below. For any commutative ring $A$, $t\in A$, and $Q=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, there is an $A_t$-algebra isomorphism $Q_t\cong A_t[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ sending $p/t^e$ to $t^{-e}\bar p$. Indeed, the polynomial universal property extends $A\to A_t$ and the variables to a map $Q\to A_t[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$; the ring localization universal property extends it to $Q_t$. Conversely, the coefficient map $A_t\to Q_t$ and the elements $x_i/1$ define a polynomial map back. The composites fix all coefficients and variables, and all fractions, so are identities. If $N$ is a $Q$-module, its localization at the constant $t\in Q$ is its underlying $A$-module localization: the equivalence relation is in both cases $t^k(t^{e'}m-t^em')=0$, and the action of $x_i$ is $x_i(m/t^e)=(x_im)/t^e$. Thus the identification respects the specified polynomial action.

source.place: Tag 051X (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-localize), polynomial specialization of its localized pairs; Tag 00CP (proposition-universal-property-localization) and Definition 07JZ (definition-localization-module).

proof.text: Goodness persists under further principal localization. More precisely, let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $N$ be an $A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$-module free over $A$ and finitely presented over that polynomial ring, and let $t\in A$. The isomorphism $N\otimes_A A_t\cong N_t$, $m\otimes(b/t^e)\mapsto bm/t^e$, and preservation of freeness under base change show that $N_t$ is free over $A_t$, with the localized images of any given basis of $N$. Apply preservation of finite presentation under localization instead over $Q=A[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with multiplicative set the powers of its constant $t$. Step 1 identifies the resulting module and ring with $N_t$ and $A_t[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Hence $N_t$ has both required good properties. No finite rank over $A$ is used.

source.place: Tag 051X (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-localize), converse: preservation of equation-flat-and-finitely-presented on further localization; Tag 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization) for the module comparison.

proof.text: For $a,h\in R$ and $r\geq0$, put $g=a/h^r\in R_h$. The ring $R_{ah}$ makes both $h$ and $a$ invertible: their inverses are $a/(ah)$ and $h/(ah)$. Thus it receives the successive localization $(R_h)_g$. Conversely, in $(R_h)_g$, both $h$ and $a=gh^r$ are invertible, so $ah$ is invertible and the map from $R$ extends from $R_{ah}$. The composites fix $R$ and hence, by uniqueness in the localization universal property, are identities. The same argument with the module universal property gives $(M_h)_g\cong M_{ah}$: its forward map sends $(m/h^s)/g^k$ to $h^{rk}h^{-s}a^{-k}m$ in $M_{ah}$, and its reverse map sends $m/(ah)^k$ to $(m/h^k)/(a/1)^k$. The maps extend the identity on $M$; uniqueness proves that their composites are identities. They respect scalars and the polynomial action, since multiplication by each $x_i$ commutes with these scalar inverses. The ring isomorphism extends coefficientwise to the polynomial rings. In particular, taking $r=0$ also gives $(R_h)_{a/1}\cong R_{ah}\cong(R_a)_{h/1}$ and the corresponding polynomial-module identifications.

proof.text:
Let $q\in G_{R_h}(M_h)$ and let $p\in D(h)$ be its contracted prime in $R$. Choose a witnessing $g\in R_h\setminus q$ and write $g=a/h^r$. Since $h/1$ is a unit, $g
otin q$ is equivalent to $a/1
otin q$, hence to $a
otin p$. Together with $h
otin p$, primality gives $ah
otin p$. By step 3 the good module $(M_h)_g$ and its base and polynomial rings are isomorphic to $M_{ah}$, $R_{ah}$ and $R_{ah}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Carry a basis along these isomorphisms to obtain an $R_{ah}$-basis; carry a finite presentation along them by applying the ring isomorphism to its matrix coefficients. This preserves exactness because these are bijections. Therefore $ah$ witnesses $p\in G_R(M)$, proving the forward inclusion into $D(h)\cap G_R(M)$.

source.place: Tag 051X (lemma-generic-flatness-locus-localize), first paragraph of proof, with its f renamed h and its h renamed ah.

proof.text: Conversely, let $p\in D(h)\cap G_R(M)$ and let $q\in\operatorname{Spec}(R_h)$ be its corresponding prime. Choose a good $a\in R\setminus p$, so $M_a$ is free over $R_a$ and finitely presented over $R_a[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. Apply step 2 over $A=R_a$ to $N=M_a$ and $t=h/1$. Both good properties hold for $(M_a)_{h/1}$. Step 3 identifies this polynomial module with $(M_h)_{a/1}$, with the corresponding base rings identified; freeness and a finite presentation pass along those isomorphisms as in step 4. Finally $a/1\notin q$ because $q$ contracts to $p$. Consequently $a/1$ witnesses $q\in G_{R_h}(M_h)$. The two inclusions give the asserted equality under contraction of primes.
